opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the basic picture is this. When a transformer produces a single token, there's a fixed number of layers the computation has to pass through. Maybe something like a hundred sequential steps, depending on the model. Within one forward pass, whatever reasoning the model does has to fit inside that fixed serial depth. It can do a huge amount in parallel at each layer, since there's a lot of width, but the number of steps that can depend on earlier steps is bounded.

Compare that to a human thinking about a problem for a few seconds. Neurons are slow, but a person can still chain together a fairly long sequence of dependent thoughts without writing anything down. Transformers are in some sense shallow in that serial sense. They're very wide, they know an enormous amount, and they can pattern-match and retrieve really effectively. But if a task needs many dependent steps, like several hops of inference, or tracking state through a long chain, the model often can't do it "in its head" within one token.

The way models get around this is chain of thought. They write out intermediate reasoning, and every token they output can be read back in. That effectively turns the text into working memory and lets serial depth scale with the number of tokens. That's a big part of why reasoning models trained with RL to think at length got so much better at math and coding.

This matters a lot for safety, which is why I care about it. If models are shallow in this sense, then a lot of the sophisticated cognition, including anything like scheming or planning to undermine oversight, would plausibly have to show up in the chain of thought. That's potentially a big monitoring opportunity. You can read the reasoning, or have another model read it, and catch things.

But I want to be careful not to overstate it. First, "shallow" is relative. Models are getting better at doing more within a single forward pass, and we see meaningful multi-hop reasoning happening internally, just less reliably than with explicit reasoning. Second, the chain of thought isn't guaranteed to be faithful. Models can do some of the work silently, and training pressure, like optimizing against a monitor, could push the visible reasoning to be less informative. Third, architectures could change. People are exploring recurrence, or reasoning in latent vectors rather than text, which would erode this property.

So my view is that it's a real and currently quite useful feature of today's systems. Right now a lot of the hard thinking is legible-ish. But we shouldn't assume it'll stay that way, and we should be deliberate about preserving it while it lasts and making the most of it.

r001.rationale: The response says that producing a single token requires computation through a fixed number of layers, limiting serial computation.

r002.rationale: It describes reading prior output tokens back in, but does not explain the specific limitation that an earlier layer at a later token cannot access later-layer hidden states from a previous token.

r003.rationale: It explains that writing intermediate reasoning as tokens and reading them back lets serial depth scale with the number of tokens, beyond the fixed depth of one forward pass.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that a transformer is basically a fixed-depth circuit. You have some number of layers, say 80 or 100 or whatever, and when you process a token, the computation that produces the next token goes through those layers once, in sequence, and that's it. There's no loop inside the forward pass. So for any single token, the amount of serial computation the model can do is bounded by the depth of the network. It can do an enormous amount of stuff in parallel at each layer, it's very wide, but the number of sequential steps where one result feeds into the next is small. Something like a hundred steps, if you're generous about what counts as a step.

And that's kind of a weird regime compared to how we normally think about computation. A human brain is also pretty shallow in some sense, neurons are slow, you only get maybe a few hundred serial firings in a second, but the brain runs for a long time and loops back on itself. A normal computer program can have a loop that runs a billion times. A transformer forward pass can't do that. If some problem genuinely requires, you know, a thousand sequential dependent steps, there's no way to fit it into one forward pass, no matter how many parameters you have.

So where does the depth come from? It comes from the tokens. Each time the model emits a token and then reads it back in, that's effectively one more serial step. Chain of thought is basically the model using its own output as scratch memory to get around the shallowness of the architecture. And that's a big part of why reasoning models work the way they do: the recurrence is happening in the context window rather than inside the weights.

I think this matters for a couple of reasons. One is that it tells you something about what these models are good at out of the box. Things that can be done in a few steps of pattern matching, where the right answer is sort of a shallow function of the input, those are easy, and the model's huge width lets it have an enormous amount of knowledge and heuristics ready at each step. Things that need long dependent chains of reasoning are hard unless you externalize them into text. And it's part of why the models can seem so impressive on some tasks and so oddly bad on others. A task that's trivial for a human who just thinks for a minute might require more serial steps than the model gets in one pass.

The other reason it matters, and this is the part I care about more, is that it's one of the stronger arguments for why current models are more legible than they might otherwise be. If the serial compute per token is small, then the model mostly can't do a lot of hidden deliberation inside a forward pass. If it needs to reason through something complicated, it kind of has to do that in the chain of thought where we can see it. That's not a guarantee. The models can do a surprising amount in a single pass, and there's always the question of how much reasoning is being done in the residual stream across many tokens in ways that don't show up in the text. But the structural fact that the architecture is shallow gives you some reason to think that heavy-duty reasoning will leak out into the tokens.

The caveat I'd add is that I don't think this is a permanent property of AI. It's a property of the current architecture and of the fact that it's really efficient to train on GPUs this way. People could build models with more recurrence, or train models to do more of their reasoning in a latent space, and some of those directions are being explored. So I'd treat the shallowness as a contingent feature that's useful right now, rather than something fundamental to what these systems have to be.

r002.rationale: It does not explain that an earlier layer at a later token cannot access later-layer hidden states from a previous token.

r003.rationale: It explains that emitting tokens and reading them back adds serial steps, with chain of thought serving as scratch memory beyond a single forward pass.

astra-6.text:
The basic sense is that a transformer has a fixed number of layers, and so it can only do a fixed amount of sequential computation to produce its next token. You might have an enormous amount of computation happening in parallel within each layer, but that’s different from being able to take the result of one step, think about it, take another step, and keep doing that for as long as the problem requires.

So if you give it a problem that really requires a thousand sequential steps, making the model wider doesn’t obviously let it do those steps in a hundred layers. It might learn a shortcut, or it might already know something very close to the answer. But there’s a constraint there on how much sequential reasoning it can do in a single forward pass.

The important qualification is that generating multiple tokens lets it get around this to some extent. If it writes out intermediate work, each new token gets another pass through the network, and it can use the previous tokens as a kind of working memory. So the claim isn’t that a transformer-based system can’t do deep computation. It’s that a single forward pass is shallow, and doing a longer computation requires something like reasoning across multiple tokens.

r001.rationale: It says the fixed number of layers limits how much sequential computation the model can do to produce its next token.

r002.rationale: It does not explain that a later token’s earlier layer cannot access a previous token’s later-layer hidden states.

r003.rationale: It explains that intermediate work in generated tokens gives each new token another network pass, enabling longer sequential computation than one pass.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic sense is that a transformer does a fixed amount of sequential computation for each token it produces. It has some number of layers, and information passes through those layers once. So if a problem requires a long chain of dependent steps, the model can’t just keep running internally until it’s finished. It has to fit that computation into its fixed depth, or spread the computation across multiple output tokens.

That’s different from having an arbitrary program that can run a loop for as long as it needs to. A transformer can do a huge amount of computation in parallel, but parallel computation doesn’t necessarily help if you need the result of one step before you can start the next.

There’s an important qualification here, which is that generating tokens gives the model a way to do more sequential computation. If it writes out intermediate reasoning, each new token gets another pass through the network and can depend on the previous tokens. So the claim isn’t that a transformer-based system can’t do long computations. It’s that a single forward pass has a limited amount of sequential depth, and that can make reasoning out loud quite useful.

r001.rationale: It says each token gets a fixed amount of sequential computation, limited by the model’s number of layers.

r002.rationale: It does not explain what an earlier layer at a later token can access from a previous token.

r003.rationale: It explains that each generated intermediate token gets another network pass and can depend on prior tokens, allowing more sequential computation than one forward pass.
